questions.learningObjective: Explain how base composition affects DNA melting temperature
questions.stem: During a structural review, the team must explain to a client why two DNA molecules of equal length melt at different temperatures.

answer.exemplar: Melting temperature depends on base composition as well as length. G-C pairs form three hydrogen bonds and stack more strongly than A-T pairs, so a molecule rich in G-C needs more heat to separate the strands. Two molecules of equal length therefore melt at different temperatures if their G-C content differs, and this difference is measured by comparing the temperature at which half the strands have separated.

questions.explanation: A strong answer links melting temperature to G-C content, since G-C pairs form three hydrogen bonds and stack more strongly than A-T pairs, and notes that length alone cannot explain it.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a carbon skeleton alters molecular behaviour
questions.stem: Consultants drafting a materials specification must justify why two molecules sharing a functional group behave differently inside a sealed reactor.

answer.exemplar: Functional groups describe local reactive chemistry, but behaviour in the reactor also depends on the carbon skeleton that carries them. A longer skeleton changes the hydrophobic surface, raises the boiling point and shifts intermolecular contacts, while a branched skeleton packs less efficiently than a straight one. questions.explanation: A strong answer argues that the carbon skeleton alters shape, size and hydrophobic surface, so the same functional group behaves differently on a branched chain. It also names boiling point and solubility.
questions.hint: Consider shape, length and hydrophobicity of the skeleton.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a rigid steroid film is less gas permeable than an oil
questions.stem: Packaging designers must explain to a client why a rigid steroid-based film is less permeable to gas than an oil of the same thickness.

answer.exemplar: A steroid has a fused, largely planar ring system, so its molecules are rigid and flat. These flat faces stack face to face and make strong van der Waals contacts, giving the material a high melting point, high stiffness and a dense, tightly packed structure. Gas molecules therefore meet few free volume sites and must diffuse through a dense, ordered lattice, which makes the film far less permeable than a floppy, disordered oil of the same thickness.

questions.explanation: A strong answer describes the fused rigid planar rings that stack face to face, giving a dense ordered lattice with little free volume, and links that packing to low gas permeability and high stiffness.
questions.hint: Think about what the flat fused rings allow to stack.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why one substrate is cleaved and a similar one is not
questions.stem: A client asks why one engineered enzyme can cut a specific linker in a fusion protein but leaves a similar second linker untouched.

answer.exemplar: Enzymes are specific because the shape and chemical properties of the active site complement those of their substrate. questions.explanation: A strong answer states that the active site shape and chemistry must complement the intended linker so it binds in the right orientation, and that a different side chain prevents that alignment.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why cholesterol and steroid hormones share a classification
questions.stem: Medicine developers must explain why cholesterol and the steroid sex hormones are classified within the same chemical group.

answer.exemplar: Cholesterol and the steroid sex hormones share the same characteristic scaffold: four fused carbon rings, three of them six-membered and one five-membered, with side chains attached at particular positions. The hormones differ from cholesterol mainly in the side chains and in the groups attached to the nucleus, which is why they are grouped as steroids despite their different roles.

questions.explanation: A strong answer names the shared four fused ring nucleus as the defining feature, and explains that differences lie in the side chains and attached groups rather than in the core scaffold.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how selective inhibition of one enzyme arises
questions.stem: Field testing reveals a compound that inhibits one of two closely similar enzymes in a soil extract while leaving the other active.

answer.exemplar: Selective inhibition arises because the inhibitor resembles the natural substrate of one enzyme and fits that enzyme's active site, competing for the site and blocking turnover. The other enzyme has a differently shaped or chemically distinct active site, so the inhibitor does not fit there and is not bound. Lock-and-key or induced-fit models both allow this discrimination, which is why a related compound can be a potent inhibitor of one pathway while leaving a parallel pathway running.

questions.explanation: A strong answer explains that the inhibitor mimics the substrate and occupies the active site of the matching enzyme, while the other enzyme's differently shaped site excludes it.
questions.hint: Think about the inhibitor competing for an active site.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why identical groups can give different solubilities
questions.stem: Junior engineers ask why two molecules carrying identical functional groups can show very different solubilities in the same water sample.

answer.exemplar: Functional groups determine the polar and reactive parts of a molecule, but the carbon skeleton sets how much nonpolar surface those groups are attached to. A molecule with a short skeleton keeps a high ratio of polar group to nonpolar area, so water can hydrate it and it dissolves readily. The same group on a long skeleton is diluted by a large hydrophobic region, so hydrophobic interactions dominate and the molecule becomes poorly soluble even though its functional group is unchanged.

questions.explanation: A strong answer explains that the skeleton changes the ratio of polar group to nonpolar surface, so the same group hydrates well on a short chain but is diluted on a long one, changing solubility.
questions.hint: Consider the ratio of polar group to nonpolar surface.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Justify a cholesterol coating as a moisture barrier
questions.stem: Design teams must justify using a cholesterol-based coating to slow moisture loss from a food wrapper over a long shelf life.

answer.exemplar: Cholesterol is built on the steroid nucleus of four fused rings, so its molecules are rigid and flat rather than floppy like the hydrocarbon chains of a triglyceride. Flat molecules stack face to face and make strong van der Waals contacts with one another, producing a dense, ordered film with little free space. Water molecules meet very few free volume sites and must diffuse through a tightly packed lattice, which slows the movement of moisture across the wrapper.

questions.explanation: A strong answer links the rigid fused ring system to flat stacking and tight packing, then explains that a dense lattice with little free volume slows water diffusion through the film.
questions.hint: Consider how the flat rings pack in the film.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish specificity from selectivity
questions.stem: Junior scientists ask why an enzyme is described as specific rather than merely selective, and request a clear distinction.

answer.exemplar: Specificity is a statement about how tightly an enzyme's active site fits one substrate or one class of related substrates, and it is a property of the enzyme itself. Selectivity is a comparative statement about a particular reaction mixture, describing which of several competing substrates is actually turned over fastest under the conditions used. A highly specific enzyme is therefore usually selective, but a selective result in one experiment does not prove that the enzyme is specific, since the outcome may reflect pH, temperature, or competitor concentrations.

questions.explanation: A strong answer distinguishes the enzyme's own active site complementarity from the outcome in a particular mixture, noting that pH, temperature and competitors can also change which substrate is used fastest.
questions.hint: Separate a property of the enzyme from an outcome.
